title: Astrid and the Portrait
premise: Ulyana Winterbourne, a pest controller who prides herself on rational explanations, is hired to deal with 'something with fingerprints' haunting the derelict Ashgrove estate. The fingerprints belong to no living person, and when she sets up sleep-recording equipment to debunk the claims, the tapes capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud—questions about Ulyana herself. As she digs into the house's history, she learns the entity feeds on belonging: it becomes whoever the household most needs, and it has decided it needs her. In the climax, Ulyana must refuse the portrait of her own face waiting in the attic—painted decades before her birth—and burn the invitation that summoned it, escaping at sunrise but carrying its voice home inside her memory, where it will wait.
about_author: Coral Zhou is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent years cataloguing estate sales and unclaimed heirlooms. She writes horror about houses that remember their owners better than the owners do.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Ulyana's POV. She takes a routine call to Ashgrove estate—a family reporting scratches and 'fingerprints' on interior glass. She mocks the superstition privately, establishing her hard-nosed skepticism. Emotional beat: controlled contempt masking exhaustion with a life spent invisible in other people's basements.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Ulyana inspects the house and finds handprints pressed into window glass—from the inside, at heights no child could reach, with whorls that don't match any human pattern she knows. She photographs them anyway, telling herself it's for the invoice. Beat: the first hairline crack in her certainty.

chapters.title: The Winterbournes
chapters.summary: She meets the last residents: an elderly brother and sister, Edith and Marcus, who speak of the house as if it were a relative. They mention a portrait in the attic they've never dared move. Beat: unease; the siblings' affection for the house reads as devotion or hostage syndrome.

chapters.title: Equipment
chapters.summary: To prove the noises are vermin settling in the walls, Ulyana installs recording equipment in the bedrooms overnight, planning to bill them for rodent proofing. POV stays with her as she works alone after dark. Beat: professional confidence curdling as the house feels watchful.

chapters.title: First Night
chapters.summary: Ulyana reviews the recordings at dawn: breathing, floorboards—and then a second voice, low and patient, answering questions. But no one asked anything aloud. The voice says her name once. Beat: cold dread; her framework offers no explanation and she hates how much she wants one.

chapters.title: Debunking
chapters.summary: She researches audio pareidolia, cross-talk, radio interference—anything. Her notes grow frantic while her daytime work suffers. A colleague notices she hasn't slept. Beat: denial doubling down; the reader sees her isolation beginning.

chapters.title: Edith's Story
chapters.summary: Edith tells her about the original Winterbournes, who commissioned a portrait of 'whoever the house was waiting for' in 1911. Every generation, someone swears the face changes. Marcus refuses to discuss it and leaves the room. Beat: belonging reframed as something sinister—the house keeps people.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Night two of recordings: the voice holds a full conversation with itself, asking and answering, reconstructing details of Ulyana's childhood—her mother's lullaby, the smell of her grandmother's kitchen. No one alive knows these things. Beat: violation; the horror turns intimate.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Ulyana tries to quit the job. Driving away, she finds a handprint on her windshield—inside the glass. She returns because there is nowhere the house isn't. Beat: the trap closes; invisibility, her armor, has failed.

chapters.title: Records
chapters.summary: At the county archive, she pulls the estate's history: a daughter, Astrid Winterbourne, who died in 1911 and was never painted. Or rather—every portrait meant for Astrid arrived already showing someone else's face. Beat: dread deepening through history; the pattern repeats across a century.

chapters.title: Marcus Confesses
chapters.summary: Marcus admits he heard the voice as a boy and answered it once. His sister never aged past what the house needed her to be. He begs Ulyana not to go to the attic. Beat: pity and terror; Marcus is a man hollowed out by belonging.

chapters.title: Questions
chapters.summary: The voice begins speaking directly to Ulyana during waking hours now, polite, reasonable, offering the thing she's always lacked: someone who knows her completely. She argues with it like a skeptic arguing a con artist. Beat: temptation; the reader half-wants her to say yes.

chapters.title: Sleep Recording
chapters.summary: Ulyana records herself sleeping deliberately. The tape captures her own voice answering the questions in a language she doesn't recognize—and agreeing to something. She cannot remember the conversation. Beat: loss of self-sovereignty; the corruption of memory begins.

chapters.title: Gaps
chapters.summary: Hours vanish from her days. She finds mud on her boots matching the attic stairs, wax under her fingernails. Edith looks at her with terrible recognition. Beat: body horror of the mind; she is becoming someone the house remembers.

chapters.title: The Portrait's History
chapters.summary: Research montage: each previous 'pest controller,' governess, and caretaker who stayed past three nights appears in old photographs standing beside the changing portrait, wearing its subject's clothes. None have graves. Beat: rising tension; the mechanism revealed.

chapters.title: Edith's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dying Edith confesses she invited the house to take her sister's place years ago and it refused—she wasn't wanted. It wants someone with nothing anchoring them. She gives Ulyana the original invitation document. Beat: guilt and revelation; belonging can be weaponized.

chapters.title: Attic Door
chapters.summary: Night falls early. The doors seal; the voice explains, gently, that sunrise is a formality and the house only needs her consent, freely given. Ulyana climbs toward the attic anyway, invitation papers in hand. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Astrid
chapters.summary: In the attic, the portrait shows Ulyana's face, aged forty years, serene. Astrid's presence finally speaks plainly: it was never the dead girl—it is the house's hunger wearing her name, and it has been lonely for a century. Beat: climax begins; empathy weaponized against her.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: The voice offers her a place, a history, a family that remembers her. Ulyana nearly accepts—then realizes acceptance means becoming another face it wears out. She strikes a match to the invitation. The house screams through every wall. Beat: climax; refusal as survival.

chapters.title: Burning
chapters.summary: Chaos: portraits igniting, the siblings' rooms emptying of warmth, the second voice fracturing into dozens of stolen voices begging. Ulyana burns the invitation and the attic portrait together as the windows break open toward dawn. Beat: cathartic destruction at great cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Ashgrove stands silent and ordinary. Edith dies peacefully within the week; Marcus moves to a flat by the sea and thanks Ulyana without understanding why. She bills the estate for rodent proofing. Beat: bittersweet resolution; the world resumes its rational shape.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Ulyana's POV, late at night in her own flat. Reviewing her old tapes one last time, she hears the second voice answer a question she hasn't asked yet—one about whether she'd like company. She presses stop. The recorder plays on. Beat: chilling coda; memory is a door that doesn't fully close.
